sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Lincoln County
sections.html:
The Lincoln County Tax Department is on the third floor at 100 East Main Street in Lincolnton. Five divisions share the work: Land Records (maps and 9-1-1 addresses), GIS, Appraisal, Listing and Collections.

The Tax Administrator is responsible for listing, appraising and assessing all real and personal property and for collecting what is owed. The same office processes exemption and exclusion requests. For revaluation questions, call the Appraisal staff at (704) 736-8670.

The department values property at true market value, meaning what a knowledgeable buyer and seller would agree on with no pressure on either side. The county applies the uniform appraisal standards in G.S. 105-283.

Bills go out each July to whoever held title on January 1. The due date is September 1. Payment stays penalty-free through January 5, or through the next business day if January 5 falls on a weekend.

An account still open on January 6 picks up a 2 percent penalty. After that, three-fourths of one percent is added on the first day of each month, and the balance becomes eligible for forced collection.

  • Pay between July 1 and August 31 and the county takes 2 percent off.
  • Commissioners set the rate by the end of June.
  • You may pay in pieces, and once this year's bill is closed you can start prepaying next year's.
  • Cash, checks, money orders, cards and e-checks all work, with a convenience fee on cards and e-checks.

Lenders with escrow accounts are not mailed notices. Most pull what they need electronically, though the borrower still gets a paper notice for personal records.

Every parcel carries the county rate of 0.499 per $100 of value, plus whatever its fire district or town levies. The county rate page prints a total for each district, so the right line depends on where the parcel sits.

A separate availability fee of $140.00 applies per major structure, and $70.00 per major structure for OAE participants. Maiden levies its own town rate, so owners there should call town hall. Where a house sits changes the bill by more than the county rate alone.

Lincoln County chose by resolution to reappraise every four years, more often than the eight-year outer limit in G.S. 105-286. The last values date from January 1, 2023, and new ones arrive on January 1, 2027.

Before each cycle, appraisers study arm's-length sales, run statistical tests, and draft a Schedule of Values that the commissioners adopt. Transfers between relatives or related companies, foreclosure sales and gifts may be set aside, since they may not show open-market prices. The 2027 Schedule of Values, Standards, and Rules has been adopted and is posted for owners.

Notices of new value usually arrive in February. The figure is meant to track market value on that January 1, so pull your parcel record before choosing an asking price. Buyers will ask what it says.

Begin with an informal review, requested within 30 days of the notice date. Email revaluation@lincolncountync.gov, use the online form, phone (704) 736-8670, or mail the Appraisal Division at 100 East Main Street, Third Floor, Lincolnton, NC 28092.

If the informal answer stands, put a written request before the Board of Equalization and Review. A separate 30-day clock starts on the informal outcome. The commissioners name five members and three alternates to that board, and G.S. 105-322 keeps its first session from falling before the first Monday of April. You hear the result in writing within a month.

After the board comes the Property Tax Commission, by written notice within 30 days, and then the Court of Appeals as the last stage. Any appeal can end with a value that is unchanged, lower or higher.

  • Helpful evidence: sales of comparable homes on or before the valuation date, similar parcels carrying lower values, photos of damage and repair bids.
  • Not grounds for appeal: high taxes, trouble paying, thin county services, or the size of the increase.
  • An outside appraisal helps only if it is dated before the valuation date, and the office does not advise buying one for this purpose.

State law gives three homestead options, and an owner can claim just one. File Form AV-9 with the county tax office. The county takes it through June 1.

  • Age or disability: an exclusion equal to the larger of $25,000 or 50 percent of appraised value, open to owners 65 and up, or those permanently and totally disabled, earning no more than $38,800 for 2026.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: the first $45,000 of appraised value is excluded, with no age or income limit.
  • Circuit breaker: a 4 percent of income ceiling when income is within the $38,800 limit, or 5 percent from there up to $58,200. The owner must have lived in the home five years, and any excess is deferred.

Landowners who farm or grow timber can ask the office about present-use value. It requires a 5-acre tract for horticulture, 10 for agriculture or 20 for forest, plus average gross income of $1,000 a year over three years for the first two uses.

The closing attorney ordinarily prorates the year's bill between the parties, so the seller bears the months of ownership. The settlement statement should show the proration, and your attorney can explain it.

Old balances do not disappear at closing. G.S. 105-355 treats the lien as attached on the listing date, and G.S. 105-374 allows a foreclosure action that works like a mortgage foreclosure and ends in a public sale at the courthouse. Redemption before confirmation costs the tax plus penalties, interest and court costs.

Some long-time owners carry an exclusion or deferral, so ask the Tax Department whether one is attached before you list. A circuit breaker deferral comes due for the previous three years when the owner sells.

Before you list, a simple routine helps. Request the balance for every open year from Collections, check your parcel record against the new values, and give your closing attorney the figures so the settlement statement matches. A cash buyer still expects the lien to be cleared at the table.

faqs.q: What date does a Lincoln County tax bill become delinquent?
faqs.a: After January 5, with the penalty beginning January 6.

faqs.q: Is there a prepayment discount in Lincoln County?
faqs.a: Yes, 2 percent off for payments between July 1 and August 31. Bills usually reach mailboxes in early July.

faqs.q: When will Lincoln County values change next?
faqs.a: January 1, 2027 is the next reset, four years after the one dated January 1, 2023. Owners normally see new notices in February.

faqs.q: Where do I send a Lincoln County value appeal?
faqs.a: Write to revaluation@lincolncountync.gov or call the Appraisal Division at (704) 736-8670 within 30 days of the notice date. If that fails, take a formal appeal to the review board.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for Lincoln County taxes at closing?
faqs.a: The seller pays through the day of closing, since the attorney splits the year. Back taxes sit as a lien on the parcel and are cleared at the table.
